source_text: Id si dubitas, evolve quae Spiritus Ecclesiis dicat. Desertam dilectionem Ephesiis imputat, stuprum et idolothytorum esum Thyatirenis exprobrat, Sardos non plenorum operum incusat, Pergamenos docentes perversa reprehendit; Laodicenos fidentes divitiis objurgat: et tamen omnes ad poenitentiam commonet, sub comminationibus quidem. Non comminaretur autem non poenitenti, si non ignosceret poenitenti. Dubium, si non et alibi hanc clementiae suae profusionem demonstrasset. Non, ait, qui ceciderit, resurget, et qui aversatus fuerit convertetur? Ille est scilicet, ille est qui misericordiam mavult quam sacrificia. Laetantur coeli, et qui illic Angeli, poenitentia hominis. Heus tu, peccator, bono animo sis, vides ubi de tuo reditu gaudeatur. Quid illa similitudinum dominicarum argumenta nobis volunt? Quod mulier drachmam perdidit et requirit, et reperit, et amicas ad gaudium invitat, nonne restituti peccatoris exemplum est? Errat et una pastoris ovicula, sed grex una carior non erat: una illa conquiritur, una pro omnibus desideratur, et tandem invenitur, et humeris pastoris ipsius refertur: multum enim errando laboraverat. Illum etiam mitissimum patrem non tacebo, qui prodigum filium revocat, et post inopiam poenitentem libens suscipit, immolat vitulum praeopimum, convivio gaudium suum oxornat. Quidni? filium enim invenerat, quem amiserat; cariorem senserat, quem lucri fecerat. Quis ille nobis intelligendus pater? Deus scilicet: tam pater nemo, tam pius nemo. Is ergo te filium suum, etsi acceptum ab eo prodegeris, etsi nudus redieris, recipiet, quia redisti, magisque de regressu tuo, quam de alterius sobrietate laetabitur, sed si poeniteat ex animo, si famem tuam cum saturitate mercenariorum paternorum compares, si porcos immundum relinquas pecus, si patrem repetas vel offensum, Deliqui, dicens, pater, nec dignus ego jam vocari tuus. Tantum relevat confessio delictorum, quantum dissimulatio exaggerat. Confessio enim satisfactionis consilium est, dissimulatio contumaciae.
pass_a_gloss: If you doubt this, unroll what the Spirit says to the Churches. He imputes deserted love to the Ephesians, reproaches the Thyatirenes for fornication and the eating of idol sacrifices, accuses the Sardians of not being full of works, reproaches the Pergamenos for teaching perverse things, rebukes the Laodicenos who are confident in their riches; and yet He exhorts all to repentance, indeed under threats. For He would not threaten the one who does not repent, if He did not forgive the one who repents. There is doubt, if He has not also demonstrated this abundance of His clemency elsewhere. Does He not say, 'The one who has fallen will rise, and the one who has turned away will be converted?' He is, to be sure, the One who prefers mercy to sacrifices. The heavens rejoice, and the Angels who are there, over the repentance of a man. Behold, you sinner, be of good cheer, you see where your return is rejoiced over. What do those arguments of the Lord's parables want to tell us? That a woman lost a drachma and sought it and found it and invited friends to rejoice, is this not an example of a restored sinner? A single sheep of the shepherd also strays, but the flock was not more precious than that one; that one is sought, that one is desired for all, and finally it is found, and it is carried back on the shepherd's own shoulders: for it had labored much by straying. I will not be silent about that very mild father, who recalls his prodigal son and gladly receives him after poverty, and after repentance, he slaughters the fatted calf, and adorns his joy with a feast. Why not? For he had found a son, whom he had lost; he had considered him more precious, whom he had made a gain. What father is this to be understood by us? God, to be sure: no one is such a father, no one is so pious. He, therefore, will receive you, His son, even if you have squandered what you received from Him, even if you return naked, because you have returned, and He will rejoice more over your return than over another's sobriety, but if you repent from the heart, if you compare your hunger with the fullness of your father's hired servants, if you leave the unclean herd of pigs, if you seek your father again, even if offended, saying, 'I have sinned, Father, and I am not worthy to be called Your son.' So much does confession of sins relieve, as much as dissimulation exaggerates. For confession is a plan of satisfaction, dissimulation is obstinacy.

pass_b_english: If you're still unsure, take a closer look at what the Spirit has to say to the churches. The Spirit calls out the Ephesians for abandoning their love, condemns the Thyatirenes for their rampant immorality and idolatry, criticizes the Sardians for their lack of action, and rebukes the Pergamenos for spreading false teachings. The Laodicenos are also scolded for trusting in their wealth, yet despite all these criticisms, the Spirit urges everyone to repent - and does so with warnings of consequences. The fact that the Spirit threatens those who refuse to repent suggests that He forgives those who do. This isn't an isolated instance, either - the Spirit's mercy is a recurring theme. As the Lord says, 'The one who has fallen will rise, and the one who has turned away will be converted' (Luke 15:11-32). It's clear that the Lord prioritizes mercy over sacrifices. The heavens and the angels rejoice when a person repents. So, take heart, sinner - your return to the fold is a cause for celebration. The parables of the Lord drive this point home. Consider the story of the woman who lost a coin and then found it, and the friends she invited to share her joy - isn't this a picture of a sinner being restored? Or think of the shepherd who leaves his flock to search for a single lost sheep, carrying it back on his shoulders once it's found. This sheep was just as precious to the shepherd as the entire flock. Then there's the father who welcomes back his prodigal son with open arms, slaughtering the fatted calf to celebrate his return. This father represents God, the ultimate example of a loving parent. If you've squandered what you've been given, if you return empty-handed, God will still receive you as His child, rejoicing more over your return than over someone else's good behavior. If you repent sincerely, comparing your poverty to the abundance of your Father's household, leaving behind the filthy ways of the world, and seeking your Father's forgiveness, even if you've offended Him, saying, 'Father, I have sinned and I'm not worthy to be called Your son,' you'll find that confession brings relief, while trying to cover up your sins only makes things worse. Confession is the first step towards making things right, while denial is just stubbornness.
